title: Bank Balance
briefing: A banking app: 12,000 requests per second, jumping to 20,000 on payday, about a minute and a half in, for about 40 seconds. 95% of requests are reads; the rest are transfers, which write to the database.

One read in five is a user checking their balance a second or two after their own transfer. If that read misses the transfer, the user sees their old balance. That counts as a failed request, a stale read, just like an error.

The primary database can't serve every read on its own. Read replicas can, but they're always a little behind the primary, and further behind when busy. Replicas can pin a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after that user writes: read-your-writes.
debrief: Sending every read to replicas shows users their old balance. A balance check comes on average 1.5 seconds after the transfer, and even a lightly loaded replica is about half a second behind, so about 3 in 10 of those checks miss the transfer.
Sending every read to the primary doesn't fit: at the payday peak that's 19,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second, 107% of the biggest database.

Read-your-writes pinning splits the difference: a user's reads within N seconds of their own write go to the primary, everything else to replicas. With a 5-second window, 96% of balance checks are pinned (1 − e^(−5 ÷ 1.5)), about 3,700 reads a second at the peak. The primary must be sized for them: with the writes, a large one is about 62% busy; a medium one would need 123%.

The window has to be longer than the worst lag, not the usual one. Two large replicas are 54% busy at normal load, about 0.4 seconds behind, but 89% busy at the peak, about 1.9 seconds behind. A 1-second window covers the normal lag and fails on payday. Worse, it leaves half the balance checks on the replicas, which pushes them to 98% busy and 10 seconds behind.

Real systems do the same with session stickiness after a write, or by having the read wait until the replica has replayed the user's last write. Either way, replica lag deserves an alert of its own: it's invisible until a spike makes it matter.

solutions.name: Replicas, with reads pinned for 5 seconds after a write
solutions.explanation: Balance checks within 5 seconds of a transfer go to the large primary, 62% busy at the peak. Everything else goes to two large replicas, which are at most 1.9 seconds behind, so the window always covers the lag.

antiSolutions.name: Every read from the replicas
antiSolutions.explanation: No pinning: a balance check right after a transfer goes to a replica about half a second behind, so 3 in 10 show the old balance. At the peak the replicas are overloaded too.

antiSolutions.name: Every read from the primary
antiSolutions.explanation: 19,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second at the peak: 107% of the biggest database.

antiSolutions.name: Pinned for 1 second
antiSolutions.explanation: Fine at normal load, when the replicas are 0.5 seconds behind. On payday the 1-second window leaves half the balance checks on replicas that fall up to 10 seconds behind.

antiSolutions.name: A medium primary
antiSolutions.explanation: The right routing, but the pinned balance checks and the writes need 123% of a medium primary at the peak.
